object.description: A wet afternoon at a crossroads in the new quarter behind the Gare Saint-Lazare. A couple under one umbrella walk towards us, the man in a top hat and frock coat, the woman veiled; a third figure, cut off by the frame, is about to collide with them, and the cobbles shine with rain all the way back to the wedge-shaped apartment block in the distance. The painting is nearly three metres wide and the figures in front are life size, so a visitor stands on the same pavement. Caillebotte, a wealthy engineer-painter who financed the group's exhibitions and bought his friends' pictures, showed it at the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877 with Renoir's Moulin de la Galette. Its careful perspective and smooth finish are not Monet's broken touch, but its subject, the ordinary modern city seen at an odd angle like a photograph, is the Impressionist subject exactly. The street layout is Haussmann's Paris, barely twenty years old when it was painted.
facts: Shown at the third Impressionist exhibition in April 1877, which Caillebotte largely organised and paid for.
The crossroads is the Place de Dublin, where the rue de Turin, rue de Moscou and rue Clapeyron meet; the buildings still stand.
212.2 by 276.2 cm, the largest canvas Caillebotte painted; bought by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1964.
Caillebotte's bequest of 1894 gave the French state the Impressionist paintings now at the heart of the Musée d'Orsay.
